subject: Automotive & EVs
title: How Seatbelts Actually Work
description: A 60-second lesson on How Seatbelts Actually Work.

hook.text: A seatbelt seems like a simple strap, but the engineering inside is surprisingly clever.

buildup.text: The retractor uses a spool and spring that lets you lean but locks during sudden motion.

discovery.text: A tiny pendulum sensor detects rapid deceleration and jams the spool in milliseconds.

twist.text: Modern pretensioners use small explosive charges to yank the belt tight the instant a crash starts.

climax.text: Load limiters then release just enough slack so the belt doesn't crack your ribs on impact.

punchline.text: Seatbelts tighten and loosen in a single crash.

quiz.question: What do pretensioners do during a crash?

details.summary: Seatbelts work by spreading crash forces across the strongest parts of the human body, the chest and pelvis, while a pretensioner and load limiter fine-tune the restraint during impact.
details.whyItMatters: The three-point seatbelt is the single most effective safety device ever invented for cars, reducing fatality risk by roughly 45 percent in frontal crashes and 60 percent in rollovers.
takeaways: The belt locks via an inertia reel during sudden deceleration
Pretensioners tighten the belt milliseconds into a crash
Load limiters ease belt force to prevent chest injuries

faq.question: What is the difference between a pretensioner and a load limiter?
faq.answer: A pretensioner fires a small pyrotechnic charge to pull the seatbelt snug against the body at the start of a crash. A load limiter then allows slight belt extension to prevent the force from cracking ribs.

faq.question: Are seatbelts effective in rear-end collisions too?
faq.answer: Yes. In a rear impact the body is pushed forward into the seat, but seatbelts prevent occupants from rebounding into the dashboard or being thrown from the vehicle in multi-impact scenarios.
